comparedAgainst: search results for "what happens when you type a url in the address bar" and "how the internet works DNS TCP TLS HTTP step by step" (GeeksforGeeks, Medium, dev.to, networkacademy.io, ExpressVPN listicles; snippets read)
justification: Formed a fresh judgement before opening rounds 1-3. I re-fetched MDN's 'How browsers work' in full: its network section is short prose with a round-trip count (DNS 1, TCP 3, TLS 5, 8 before the request) that is explicitly pre-TLS-1.3, no code, no measurements, no per-claim citations; ~85% of the page is rendering, not networking. I re-fetched gec.dev's 'How web requests work' in full: a well-organised conceptual guide with one sequence diagram, no runnable code, no measured timings, no RFC citations, ~7-minute read. Fresh SERP snippets for both target queries return only generic five-step listicles (DNS -> TCP -> request/response -> render) with unsourced round-numbers. This article remains clearly superior in original value: it reproduces every step from C# (Uri parsing, a localhost-warm-up-isolated DNS timing, hand-typed HTTP over TcpClient with real chunked-framing bytes, the same request through SslStream with per-band timings across six runs, a one-IP/three-names SNI experiment with real refusals, a loopback capture of what HttpClient actually sends, a TTL-based hop counter with disclosed run-to-run variance, and a NoDelay/Nagle measurement with disclosed exceptions), derives the 56->78->118 byte encapsulation arithmetic from cited RFC sections, and explicitly corrects the outdated pre-1.3 TLS story that MDN itself still tells. Plagiarism check: five distinctive sentences ('is four separate conversations', 'TLS exists to make the conversation unreadable...', 'IP is where the network stops making promises', 'Round-trip time is set by distance... buying more bandwidth does not reduce it', 'the response that took four round trips to fetch is a list of further things to fetch') were searched in quotes; none matched any existing page, confirming the prose is original, not paraphrase. Structure is not templated: headings ('Band 1: the name becomes an address', 'Where the time went', etc.) name their content and are unlike big-o-notation's or binary-search's heading sets (checked both fresh); exercise forms (plan-from-URL, delete-a-header, take-NoDelay-away, measure-reuse, find-the-failed-band) vary in kind, not just topic. No filler intro/outro; the page ends on a diagnostic exercise. No keyword stuffing. Round-3 findings, re-verified in the current file rather than assumed fixed: the duplicated 'Header names are case-insensitive' sentence now appears exactly once (grep-confirmed); the DNS-speed paragraph now reads 'which points to a stored answer somewhere between this machine and the recursive resolver, either in the operating system's own cache or in a resolver on the path; this program cannot tell which layer answered', matching the callout instead of contradicting it; the unsourced NAPT prevalence phrase ('as it commonly does between a home network and the internet') is gone, leaving only the cited RFC 3022 behaviour; the 'Band N' heading gap is closed ('Bands 2 and 4: TCP and HTTP without TLS') and the intro now correctly says bands 1 and 3 each get their own program while 2 and 4 share one. All four are genuinely fixed, not just claimed fixed. Still open, carried from rounds 1-3: docs/INTEGRATOR_REQUESTS.md still has no entry for the six wanted networking glossary terms and src/content/glossary/ still has no DNS/TCP/TLS/RTT/port/packet files, though the crosslinks file has listed the wanted terms since round 1 -- three rounds have not produced the request itself. This is a real gap (the pillar's entry page has no glossary ties, unlike sibling pillars) but it is an internal information-architecture nicety, not something a Google policy reviewer would read as low-value content: the page is not a navigation dead end (the 'After the last byte of HTML' section and 'Keep reading' block both work, and the crosslinks file is sensible), so it stays minor. New, from my own fresh read: two general behavioural claims still carry no citation and are broad enough to be worth a source or a hedge -- 'buying more bandwidth does not reduce [round-trip time]' and 'the others are alternatives if the connection fails' (about unused DNS answers) -- both plausible and uncontroversial to an informed reader but exactly the class of claim the brief asks to source or scope. Neither rises above a nit: they are well short of the kind of unsupported claim that damaged earlier rounds (the round-1 DoH/ALPN-ordering claims, the round-2/3 NAPT prevalence claim), which are all gone now. Net: with every prior writer-owned issue verified fixed and no new major problem found, the article's remaining defects are two small citation nits and one persistent integrator-side gap, none of which is a policy risk or a low-value signal; a reviewer hunting for thin or mass-produced content would not flag this page, and it is now closer to the round-2 high-water mark (8.8) than to round 3's dip.

issues.location: 'Where the time went', paragraph after the table: 'Round-trip time is set by distance and the networks in between, and buying more bandwidth does not reduce it.'
issues.problem: A general networking claim (RTT is bounded by propagation delay, not throughput) stated with no citation. Uncontroversial to an informed reader, but the brief asks for a primary source on every non-obvious factual claim, and this one is doing real work in the article's argument for why connection reuse and multiplexing matter more than bandwidth.
issues.fixLooksLike: Cite a primary/textbook source for the propagation-vs-bandwidth distinction (e.g. Kurose & Ross's transmission-vs-propagation-delay treatment, or an RFC/IETF document that states it), or soften to 'On a given path, round-trip time is set mostly by distance, and more bandwidth does not shorten it' with a citation, or drop the clause if no source is opened for it.

issues.location: 'Band 1: the name becomes an address', last paragraph: 'A name can map to several addresses, as it did here. The client picks one and moves on; the others are alternatives if the connection fails.'
issues.problem: A general claim about client fallback behaviour with no citation, and not demonstrated by the program above it, which only ever uses found[0] and never falls back to found[1..]. It reads as a fact about DNS clients in general rather than something this page's code shows.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either cite the fallback behaviour (e.g. .NET's SocketsHttpHandler/Happy-Eyeballs documentation, or RFC 8305) or rescope to what is true here: 'A name can map to several addresses, as it did here; this program uses only the first one, but a real client that fails to connect to it would try the next.'
